Reserves of cannel and bituminous coal are not extensive enough to support a coal-fired electric generating plant. Recent estimates of near surface potential lignite resources in Texas (Kaiser, 1974) include 129 million short tons of relatively low grade lignite in the Indigo formation, Wilcox Group, in extreme southeastern Maverick County and extreme western Dimmit County.
Rio Grande and Tributaries
2.13 Rio Grande. The Rio Grande flows in a southeast direction across the south central part of Colorado, turns south as it enters New Mexico and flows across New Mexico past the cities of Santa Fe, Albuquerque, and Las Cruces. Near Las Cruces, the Rio Grande swings to the southeast and continues to flow in this general direction until it enters the Gulf of Mexico about 20 miles east of Brownsville, Texas. On its course from Las Cruces to Brownsville, the Rio Grande flows past the Texas cities of El Paso, Del Rio, Eagle Pass, Laredo, and Brownsville, and it forms the 1,240 mile long international boundary with Mexico.
2.14 Principal tributary streams entering the Rio Grande below El Paso are the Rio Conchos, Rio Salado, and Rio San Juan from the Mexican side and the Pecos River and Devils River from the United States side. The Rio Conchos enters the Rio Grande near Presidio, Texas. The Pecos River and Devils River flow into Amistad Reservoir. Falcon Reservoir receives the flows of the Rio Salado. The Rio San Juan confluence with the Rio Grande is 40 miles downstream from Falcon dam near Rio Grande City, Texas. Very little flow is contributed from the Rio Grande basin above Fort Quitman, Texas, and from the Pecos River basin above Red Bluff Dam. Fort Quitman is on the Rio Grande about 80 river miles below El Paso. Red Bluff Dam is on the Pecos River near the Texas-New Mexico border.
2.15 Between Fort Quitman and the mouth of San Francisco Creek south of Sanderson, Texas, the Rio Grande follows a sinuous course through a series of very deep canyons alternating with narrow valleys. The fall of the river in this reach is about 4/2 to 
6\frac{1}{2}
 feet per mile. Below the mouth of San Francisco Creek and continuing to near Del Rio, the Rio Grande flows within a moderately deep, meandering canyon and the fall of the river is gradually reduced until it is about 3 feet per mile near Del Rio. Below Del Rio and continuing to the Gulf of Mexico, the river flows with a much broader, less incised valley and the fall of the river continues to be gradually reduced until it is essentially flat near the Gulf of Mexico. In the 1,240 mile long course of the Rio Grande between El Paso and the Gulf of Mexico, the streambed of the Rio Grande drops from an elevation of 3,720 feet at the El Paso to slightly below sea level at the mouth of the river. This is an average fall of approximately 3 feet per mile.
2.16 Historic Floods. Major floods on the Rio Grande usually occur during June, July, August or September and are normally produced by tropical storms moving inland from the Gulf of Mexico or by frontal-type thunderstorms. Records extending back to May 1900 indicate the occurrence of four major floods on the Rio Grande in the vicinity of Amistad Dam site to deliberate reservoir impoundment beginning on May 31, 1968. The peak discharge of 1,158,000 cfs reached during the flood of June 1954 at a gage about 2 miles below Amistad Dam site is the greatest rate of discharge ever recorded on the Rio Grande.
